name: Pale Infrastructure (Reissue)
description:
The 2218 archival reissue of Pale Infrastructure's 2196 debut album, originally self-released on 200 vinyl pressings that have since become collector items valued at upward of Φ 3,000 per copy. The reissue was licensed through Vantablack's heritage subsidiary Sediment Records after a decade-long legal dispute with the surviving band members, and includes the original nine tracks remastered for neural-feed delivery plus a second disc of unreleased studio sessions, two live recordings, and a forty-minute documentary audio piece assembled from interviews with the band. Pale Infrastructure dissolved in 2201 following the death of founding vocalist and lyricist Adaeze Ferreira-Kurosawa; the reissue was opposed by two of the five surviving members, who considered it exploitative.

Standout tracks from the original album include 'Mineral Rights,' a dense, slow-building piece that layers West African call-and-response vocals over cascading synthesizer arpeggios in a scale that refuses to resolve; and 'The Pale Hours,' which was later covered by seventeen different artists and became the band's most recognized piece — Ferreira-Kurosawa's original vocal performance, heard here in the remaster, is considered definitive. From the bonus material, a previously unreleased track called 'Infrastructure Hymn' is a raw, unfinished recording that sounds nothing like the polished album and everything like what the band might have become.
creator: Pale Infrastructure
audience: Long-term Pale Infrastructure fans across Circuit and Tier 3, music historians, collectors, younger listeners discovering the catalog, anyone who followed the legal dispute as a story in its own right
cultural_impact: The reissue reignited a debate within GLMZ's music community about corporate ownership of underground cultural artifacts. The two dissenting band members — Okonkwo Strand-Pietersen and Yuki Abara-Voss — gave a widely circulated interview in which they called the release 'a body dug up and dressed for someone else's party.' Sediment Records' handling of the estate was scrutinized after it emerged they had altered the liner notes to remove a dedication to a political prisoner. The original vinyl pressings have become symbols of authentic Circuit culture; owning one marks a person as either a genuine longtime fan or someone wealthy enough to perform that identity.
known_fans: musicians who cite the band as an influence
activists who followed the legal dispute
story_hooks: One of the dissenting band members is selling the master tapes of the unreleased material through back channels, intending to release a competing version of the bonus disc that includes the liner notes Sediment Records removed — Vantablack's legal team is moving to stop it.

A collector has acquired what appears to be a 201st vinyl pressing that was never officially documented, with a handwritten track listing that differs from the released album, including a song that no one in the band remembers recording.

Adaeze Ferreira-Kurosawa's death in 2201 was ruled a medical event, but one of the surviving members has recently started suggesting otherwise in interviews, and a journalist covering the story has asked the players for help obtaining documents from the band's final touring period.
